blog.title: Service Area Pages: How to Rank in More Than One California City
blog.title_tag: Service Area Pages for Local SEO: Rank in Multiple Cities | ART3RY
blog.meta_description: How to rank in more than one city without doorway pages: what Google allows, how to set service areas, and how to write city pages that earn their place.
blog.dek: You serve five cities and your website mentions one. The tempting fix is five near-identical pages, and it is the fix Google calls spam. Here is what works instead, built for California service businesses.

sections.h2: You serve five cities. Google thinks you serve one.
paragraphs: Say you run an HVAC company out of Fresno. You also drive to Clovis, Madera, Selma, and Reedley, and you would love to show up when someone in Reedley searches for a tech at 9 PM in August. But your site says Fresno on every page, your Google profile shows one pin, and the map treats you as a Fresno business. Reedley never sees you.

This is one of the most common local search gaps for California trades, because our metro areas sprawl and the work does not stop at a city line. The Central Valley especially: a thirty-minute drive is routine, and customers in smaller towns often have fewer choices, which means a decent listing wins by default.

I run a one-person California field-services company with 700+ jobs through a system I built, and I pointed that system at my own site. Organic traffic went up 60% in 28 days with zero ad spend. Here is how I think about covering more places without tripping the wire.

sections.h2: The principle: one real page for each place you really serve
paragraphs: A page earns a spot in the index by being the best answer to a specific question. A page for Reedley should exist if you genuinely do work in Reedley and you have something real to say about doing work there. If you have nothing to say but the city name swapped into a template, the page has no reason to exist, and Google knows it.
That is the whole principle. Real service, real place, real information. Everything else in this post is how to apply it.

The shortcut is obvious: copy one page, change the city name, publish thirty times. Google has a name for it. Its spam policies describe doorway abuse as pages created to rank for similar searches that [lead users to intermediate pages that are less useful than the final destination, including multiple pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies).

In plain terms: thirty pages that say the same thing about thirty towns is the thing being targeted. Best case, those pages sit unindexed and do nothing. Worst case, they drag down the pages that were doing fine. Google's broader advice is to [create helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) that gives original information and a complete answer, and a thin city page is the opposite of that.
So the question is never how many city pages you can publish. It is how many you can fill with something true that a customer in that town would value.

sections.h2: Step one: set your service areas on Google first
paragraphs: Before you touch the website, fix the profile. The Google Business Profile is what drives the map. For businesses that go to the customer, [Google lets you add up to 20 service areas by city or postal code, and says to remove your address if you do not serve customers there](https://support.google.com/business/answer/9157481). It also says service areas should stay within roughly two hours of driving from your base.

Pick the places you actually go, not the places you wish you did. If you work out of a home garage, hide the address and list the areas. Use cities and postal codes, not a made-up radius. The full checklist for the profile side is in [Google Business Profile optimization](/google-business-profile-optimization/), and the ranking mechanics are in [how to rank on Google Maps](/blog/how-to-rank-on-google-maps/).

One caution I will repeat: proximity is the factor you cannot buy. A listing based in Fresno will not beat a Reedley-based competitor for a Reedley search just by adding Reedley to the list. What adding the area does is make you eligible and relevant. The page and the reviews do the rest.

sections.h2: Step two: decide which cities deserve their own page
paragraphs: Make a short list using three tests. Do you do real, regular work there? Do people there search for what you sell? Can you write at least four hundred words that would help someone who lives there and that could not be pasted onto another city?

If a city passes all three, it gets a page. If it fails the third, it gets a mention on a broader service page, such as a list of towns you cover, rather than its own URL. For a business covering five towns, that usually means a page for the two or three where you have real jobs and photos, and a coverage list for the rest.

sections.h2: Step three: write the page like it belongs to that city
paragraphs: What makes a city page real is local proof. Describe an actual job you did there, without naming the customer. Mention the neighborhoods and landmarks you drive past, the local conditions that change the work, and the questions people there ask.

A Clovis plumbing page might cover older homes with galvanized pipe and how that changes a repair quote. A Madera landscaping page might talk about hard clay soil and water restrictions. A Modesto electrician page might discuss panel upgrades in postwar housing. These are not tricks. They are what a competent local says on the phone, and they are impossible to template.

Add the basics every page needs: what you do there, a plain way to call or book, hours, a few photos from real jobs, and two or three reviews from that area if you have them. Link each city page to the matching service page and back to the parent. If your service page for SEO or websites needs a look, the pages at [SEO](/services/seo/) and [websites](/services/websites/) show the structure I use.

sections.h2: Step four: make the structure obvious to Google
paragraphs: Build one parent page per service, such as water heater repair, and have the city pages hang off it. Link from the parent to each city page with a descriptive phrase. Use one clear heading that names the service and the city. Keep your name, address, and phone number identical everywhere they appear.

Add LocalBusiness structured data to the site so the machine-readable version matches what a person sees. [Google says only the name and address are required, and recommends adding as many properties as you can, such as hours, phone, and coordinates](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/local-business). Keep it consistent with the visible page and do not mark up things that are not there.

sections.h2: What to measure, and how long it takes
paragraphs: Watch three numbers: impressions for the city term in Search Console, calls from the profile in that area, and where new customers say they found you. A new page can take weeks to settle, and map results move on their own schedule, so judge it over a quarter, not a weekend.

If a city page gets no impressions after a few months, look at whether the page is truly different from the others, whether it is linked from somewhere that matters, and whether the city is worth chasing at all. Cutting a weak page is fine. A smaller site of real pages beats a bigger one of filler.

If you want a second pair of eyes before you publish anything, [the free diagnostic](/diagnostic/) checks which cities you should own, how you rank today, and where the easy wins sit. And if you are in the Central Valley, the [Fresno SEO](/seo-company-fresno/) page shows how I handle it for local owners.

faq.q: How many service areas can I list on Google Business Profile?
faq.a: Up to 20 cities or postal codes, according to Google's guidelines, and they should generally stay within about two hours of driving from your base. List only places you genuinely serve.

faq.q: Do I need a separate page for every city I serve?
faq.a: No. Give a city its own page only if you do real work there and can write something genuinely local that could not be pasted onto another city. Cover the rest with a coverage list on a service page.

faq.q: Are city pages considered doorway pages?
faq.a: They can be. Google's spam policies call out multiple pages targeted at specific cities that funnel users to one page. Pages that contain real local information, real jobs, and a complete answer are different from templated copies.

faq.q: Can I rank in a city where my business is not located?
faq.a: You can appear for searches there, especially for service-area work, but the map favors proximity. Strong reviews, a relevant page for that city, and a complete profile improve your chances, and you should expect it to be harder than ranking at home.

faq.q: How long do city pages take to rank?
faq.a: Expect weeks before a page settles and a few months before you can judge it fairly. Track impressions in Search Console, calls from that area, and where new customers say they found you.

blog.title: How to Show Up in AI Search as a Local Business
blog.title_tag: How to Show Up in ChatGPT and Google AI Search | ART3RY
blog.meta_description: How a local business shows up in AI search and AI Overviews: what Google actually says, what is still unproven, and the plain steps worth doing this month.
blog.dek: Customers now ask a chatbot who to hire. Nobody has a proven playbook for it yet, but the basics are not a mystery. Here is what Google says, what is guesswork, and what I would do first.

sections.h2: People are asking a machine who to hire
paragraphs: A homeowner types a question into an AI assistant: who is a good electrician near Visalia that can do a panel upgrade? Instead of ten blue links, they get a paragraph and a short list of names. If yours is not on it, you were not in the room.

That is a new door, and a lot of people are selling keys to it. Most of what gets sold is confident and unproven. I would rather tell you what is known, what is not, and what is worth doing regardless of how the technology moves.

I run a one-person California field-services company, and 700+ jobs have gone through the system I built. When I pointed that system at my own site, organic traffic rose 60% in 28 days with no ad spend. I do not have a secret trick for chatbots. I have a habit of doing the unglamorous things that every search system rewards.

sections.h2: The principle: AI search reads what regular search reads
paragraphs: Here is the most useful sentence in this whole space, and it comes from Google. On appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode, [Google says there are no additional requirements and no special optimizations necessary, and that SEO best practices remain relevant](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features).

Read that twice, because it cuts through the noise. The thing that gets you into the AI answer is mostly the thing that gets you into the normal results: pages that can be crawled, clear and useful content, accurate business information, and signs that real people trust you.

I want to be careful about scope. That statement is about Google's own AI features. Other assistants pull from different sources and Google does not speak for them. So treat everything below as the habits most likely to help across the board, not a guarantee for any one product.

sections.h2: Why this matters more for local businesses than you think
paragraphs: AI answers favor sources that look like a settled consensus. If your name, services, and city appear the same way on your site, your Google profile, and a handful of other trusted places, a system has an easy time deciding you exist and what you do. If those disagree, you become a risk, and a model that wants to give a safe answer will skip you.

There is also a speed effect. When an assistant gives one short list instead of a page of results, the gap between first place and fifth place gets wider. Being in the top few matters more than it did. That is a good reason to fix the basics now, while your competitors are still arguing about acronyms.

sections.h2: How to apply it, part one: make the facts match everywhere
paragraphs: Choose the exact way you write your business name, phone, address or service area, and hours. Use it identically on your website, your Google Business Profile, your Facebook page, and any directory that matters to your trade. Small differences like Ste versus Suite do less harm than a different phone number or a wrong city, but fix them anyway.

Keep your profile current. [Google specifically lists keeping Business Profile information up to date as part of appearing well in its AI features](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features). Holiday hours, new services, a changed number: update them the day they change. The checklist for that is in [Google Business Profile optimization](/google-business-profile-optimization/).

sections.h2: Part two: answer the actual questions in plain text
paragraphs: An assistant can only quote what is written on a page. Put the real answers in readable text: what you do, what areas you cover, what a typical job involves, how long it takes, how you handle emergencies, and what a customer should have ready when they call. Google also recommends presenting important content in text form rather than burying it in images.

Write headings that sound like questions people ask. Do you repair tankless water heaters? Do you serve Madera County? Then answer in the first sentence under the heading, and add detail below. A short FAQ section on each service page does this naturally. This is the same method I use on every post here, including [why your business is not showing up on Google](/blog/why-is-my-business-not-showing-up-on-google/).

Say specific things only you can say. A description of a job you did last month in a named neighborhood is something a model cannot find on fifty other sites, and it is the closest thing to a moat a small business has.

sections.h2: Part three: add structured data that matches the page
paragraphs: Structured data is a labeled version of your facts for machines. [Google's LocalBusiness guidance requires a name and address and recommends adding hours, phone, and location coordinates where you can](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/local-business). Add FAQ and service details that reflect what is visible on the page, and only that.

Google also says to align structured data with visible content, which is the rule that keeps this honest. If the markup says you are open on Sundays and the page says you are closed, you have created the kind of conflict that makes systems trust you less. If you use a site builder, check whether it already outputs this before you add anything. If you would rather not touch markup yourself, that is part of what a [website build](/services/websites/) should handle.

sections.h2: Part four: earn mentions from real places
paragraphs: Reviews, local news, the chamber of commerce, supplier directories, trade associations, and the occasional guest post are all places where other people vouch for you. Reviews especially: a steady flow of recent, specific ones is the strongest trust signal a local business has, and I covered how to get them in [how to get more Google reviews](/blog/how-to-get-more-google-reviews/).
Do not buy mentions or manufacture them. They are cheap to fake and easy to spot, and the penalty falls on you.

sections.h2: What is unproven, so you can ignore the hype
paragraphs: Nobody outside the companies running these systems can tell you exactly how a given assistant decides whom to recommend, and it changes. Anyone selling a guaranteed ranking inside a chatbot is guessing, or selling. There is also no reliable way yet to measure how often you are mentioned across all of them.

What you can measure: ask a few assistants the question your customer would ask, once a month, and note whether you appear. Watch Search Console for impressions on question-style searches. Ask new customers how they found you, and add a line for AI to the list. That is crude, and it is honest.

sections.h2: What I would do this month
paragraphs: Fix the facts so they match everywhere. Add a real FAQ to your top three service pages. Check your structured data. Ask your last ten happy customers for reviews. Then repeat the same small habits every month, because consistency is what compounds in search.

If you want someone to check how a search engine and an assistant currently see your business, [the free diagnostic](/diagnostic/) covers your visibility, your profile, and your site against competitors, and our [SEO](/services/seo/) service builds and maintains this for owners who would rather be working.

faq.q: How do I get my business to show up in ChatGPT?
faq.a: There is no guaranteed method. The habits most likely to help are consistent business information everywhere, clear text answers on your site, accurate structured data, and a steady flow of real reviews and mentions. Check by asking assistants the question your customers would ask.

faq.q: Do I need special optimization for Google AI Overviews?
faq.a: Google says there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and that standard SEO best practices remain relevant. Crawlable pages, useful content, and current Business Profile information are the foundation.

faq.q: Does structured data help with AI search?
faq.a: It helps machines understand your facts, and Google recommends aligning structured data with visible page content. It is not a shortcut. Use LocalBusiness markup with your real name, address, hours, and phone, and keep it consistent with the page.

faq.q: Is SEO still worth it if AI answers questions directly?
faq.a: Yes. The same fundamentals feed both, and Google says clicks from pages with AI Overviews tend to be higher quality engagement. Ranking well in normal search remains the base that AI features draw from.

faq.q: How can I tell if AI assistants recommend my business?
faq.a: Once a month, ask a few assistants the question your customer would type, such as best electrician near you, and note whether you appear. Also add AI search as an option when you ask new customers how they found you.
